To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the European Parliament has been successful in establishing a new method of interest representation, which is based on the use of soft law and the creation of a "soft law community" of interest representatives.

1) the EU legislator is increasingly using legal and para-legal instruments to shape the activities of economic actors; 2) this is due to a combination of factors, including the need to address the problems of the single market; 3) this trend is accompanied by the growing role of the European Parliament; and 4) this has an impact on the methods and strategy of interest groups, which have to adapt to the new situation.

(a) the European Parliament has a strong impact on the choice of the regulatory instrument; (b) the choice of instrument has a strong impact upon the strategies of interest representation; (c) the impact of the Parliament on the choice of instrument is mediated by interest group preferences for regulation.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the impact of the EU regulatory framework on the preferences of interest groups and the impact of interest groups' preferences on the regulatory framework.
the following questions: How do the EU institutions' preferences for soft law and for the use of new regulatory tools affect interest groups' strategies of representation?
the question of whether there is a relationship between the type of regulation and the type of governance tools used to achieve the policy objectives.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the EP's new role in EU policymaking has not been accompanied by a new role for the organized interests.
soft law has become a tool for the European Parliament to influence the EU's regulatory agenda.
soft law or no law is the European Parliament's new approach to the management of organized economic interests.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the EU's regulatory environment has become a major factor of interest representation.
the European Parliament is not yet able to fully control its own preferences and that it is not able to control the interests of the organized private sector.
the EP's new role as a political institution has an impact on the way organized interest groups operate.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the European Parliament is increasingly using soft law instruments to manage organized interests.

the EU legislator is more likely to adopt legal or para legal rules when the preferences of private actors are more heterogeneous, when there is a high degree of uncertainty about the consequences of a regulatory intervention and when there are strong incentives for private actors to lobby for a regulatory solution.
the EU is not a unitary actor and that the preferences of private interests are not unitary either.
